analysis.one_liner: Extends family and medical leave protections to nearly all workers, including new hires and small-business employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Family and Medical Leave Act lets eligible workers take unpaid, job-protected leave for things like a new baby, a serious illness, or caring for a sick parent. Today, only workers who have been on the job for at least 12 months, and only workers at companies with 50 or more employees, qualify. This bill would cut the waiting period to 90 days and cover every employer with even one employee, plus federal, congressional, and presidential staff. Millions of workers at small firms and people in their first year of a job would gain protection they don't have now.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in their first year at a job, employees of small businesses with fewer than 50 employees, and federal, congressional, and presidential employees who would no longer have to wait 12 months to qualify for unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the employment period required to qualify for family and medical leave from 12 months to 90 days, covering workers in their first year on the job, including federal, congressional, and presidential employees.
Applies the family and medical leave requirements to all employers with one or more employees, instead of only employers with 50 or more, extending job-protected leave to workers at small businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Small employers, who would bear the cost of holding jobs open and managing absences during protected leave for the first time, and larger employers, who would face leave requests from workers hired within the past year.

drawbacks.text: Extending leave coverage to every employer with even one employee means a single worker's leave can leave a tiny business without anyone to do the work, a burden the 50-employee threshold was written to avoid for the smallest firms.
The bill mandates unpaid leave only; it adds job protection but does not pay workers during leave, so many newly eligible low-wage workers still could not afford to take the time off.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for millions of workers who currently have no job protection if they need leave in their first year of work or work at a small firm. The cost side is concentrated on small employers, who face scheduling and staffing challenges with no small-firm exemption; the lack of any paid component also limits how useful the new eligibility is for the lowest-wage workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor bills, which never acted on it, and it died there when this Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the Job Protection Act on March 3, 2022, with five Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors: Elizabeth Warren, Dick Durbin, Kirsten Gillibrand, Alex Padilla, and Patty Murray.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken on it.
All six cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, especially small businesses, are better off because the bill died: they never had to extend leave coverage to new hires and single-employee firms. Workers who lack leave protections are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Job Protection Act to expand FMLA eligibility and employer coverage.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Dick Durbin, Kirsten Gillibrand, Alex Padilla, and Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never acted on it, leaving it without a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters were Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; with Republicans holding 50 Senate seats in the 117th Congress, the bill had no cross-party base to move it out of committee.

industries.industry: Small businesses with fewer than 50 employees
industries.note: The bill would have required these firms for the first time to hold jobs open during family and medical leave, a cost the current 50-employee threshold exempts them from. A single worker's leave can leave a tiny firm unstaffed, which is why the smallest employers would have borne the sharpest new burden.
Already covered by the FMLA, but the 90-day tenure change would have exposed them to leave requests from employees hired within the past year, reducing scheduling predictability.
